blocks.x: Okay, we're on. Okay, alright. Interview with June Gardner, April 17th, 1996. This is real number one. Okay. Alright. Why don't you give your birthday? That's the best thing. Okay, when I was born on December the third...
All right, this is a reel number two with June Gardner, April 17th 1996. Okay.
Yeah, well like I said.
We're back. Okay. That's uh, where did we leave off?

When I came out of the service in 53, I went back with Roy Brown. Same band? Same, well I know you had different, some different players at that particular, because they were and they would pick up different guys along the way, you know. But names get away from me.
Was it, with bands like this they seem kind of liquid, these road bands a lot of times, and you're changing players. Yeah. Was it hard to break people in?

Yeah, because everybody at the time, everybody, jazz was really coming on strong. Everybody wanted to play like Bud, play like Max, you know, and you say hey, a lot of them didn't even know the difference between the blues. Uh-huh. You know, they figured if you played the blues you wasn't playing jazz. Right. That's a particular thing. But I mean like, a lot of Roy Brown things, eight ball blues, twelve ball blues. Uh-huh. So we ran into some stars who really couldn't play, period. I mean they were bullshitting all the way, excuse the expression. But uh, what we ran.
Or somebody who could play modern jazz, but you told them to play a blues?

Yeah, like a lot of these low rhythm and blues band, they had riffs that they would play. I mean Roy Brown had riff riff riff. Yeah, you know, that, that, da, da, da, da, da, da, you know. Right. It's simple, you know, if you start, play this, you know. Right. But uh, well, most overall it was a good band because like during those times we would play maybe an hour or so before he would even come on and sing. Oh, okay. So people would be dancing and the band is hot and hitting. It was, and we'd been together for a while. It was a very tight band, you know. And so I left there and uh, stayed a, maybe uh, another year to, I was 53, yeah. Maybe to about 55. I said then I came back to New Orleans and I, uh, worked for just about all of them. Different clubs that we had here, the Shattered Lion, Nightcap. And we had a lot of clubs to, uh, play a lot, a lot of black clubs and balls. We used to work so much with just regular guys like Ray Tyler, Chuck, Eddie Collins, myself. We would have nine jobs in a week. You know, that different balls. Guys would say, man, don't take no more after this. That's how much we would work with this, with the different clubs around. Uh, you know, cause the people were coming out and enjoying themselves, you know.
This is like mid fifties?

Yes, mid fifties, early sixties. Uh, cause uh, I ended up in late, late uh, sixties. They all had Masons. Uh, I played like that, the Haven, uh, on, uh, North Clavin Street. Uh, well, yeah. Like I said, there were quite a few places that you could play. Big time, Crip, Jackson and La Salle, you know. Seals, Barb. We had a lot about, uh, the Forest Inn, first in Magnolia. This would be like Thursday nights. We had packed houses, Tuesday nights at these places. People was coming out to support a lot of music. Uh-huh. You know. And, uh, none of the sudden, jazz. We were playing jazz, but, uh, it just, it just good to see people out. Like I said, they didn't have no special night. Everybody would say, where are you playing today? I'm over here, this place. And then, uh, like I said, we used a variety of guys. You know, at the time I was the band leader. Sometime Ray Tyler would be the band leader. Chuck Beatty. We, another place we used to play all the time is Joy Tavern back in. Right. Good job. Yeah. As a matter of fact, that's where I was playing, uh, in 60, 1960, I left. I got a call for Sam, Sam Cook. Uh-huh. At Drees Mohammed, which is Leo Morris. Uh-huh. Was the first drummer with Sam, but he stayed about a month and he left. And he recommended me and they called New Orleans. Uh-huh. I was working at Joy Tavern at the time. So, in 19, at the beginning of 60. And I left New Orleans and I joined Sam. Uh-huh. And I stayed with him until he, tragic in his life, he got killed. Uh-huh. Uh, then I came back to New Orleans after he, well, they tried to get me to stay in Los Angeles. I said, no, come back home.
What, stay in Los Angeles?

Just, I mean, you know, just living, uh, because I knew a lot of the musicians. Right. And I mean, this was on bass for Sam. We used to go, be in Los Angeles. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. the way he was living at the time. And after you got killed. And you know you'd meet the musicians and say, hey man, you're going back to New Orleans? Yeah. We'll stay here, blah, blah, blah. I said, no. Well, my family was here.
And what if they said you know there was a guaranteed work for them?

Well, the them said, so you know the time you knew them the guys in the studio. I guess you would have to pay some dues, not that every door would have been open for you. Like I said, I was pretty established. I knew a lot of the studio musicians around in Earl Palmer with a very dear friend. Excuse me. So I mean, that would have been all right, but I would have had to pay some dues. But this is home.
Did you consider making the new debt?

No, well, I would have had to move my family. I had to take this under consideration. You know, see my kids were smaller at the time, and that would have been moving and giving up one thing to that. But this New Orleans is home. You know, I like that.

Okay. Reel number three with June Gardner, April 17th, 1996. Okay. I want to, before that, before we talk about drumming, some other things about your family. Your father's name's Albert, and your mother's name was? Olivia. Olivia what?
Olivia Woodland Gardner.
Woodland Gardner. Yeah. And you said you had a large family. Could you tell me who your brothers and sisters were?

My brother was Tom. My oldest brother was Tommy Gardner. My other brother was Richard Gardner. My oldest sister was Myrtle Gardner, Thelma Gardner, and Cleo Gardner. It was like six of us. I'm the only one left. Everyone else went on home. Like I said, I was a baby in an older family. They were older, you know, much older than me. But I was the last one. And I'm 65.
What about your grandfather? Do you know anything about your grandfather?
God bless him. I never really had anything to him. Like I said, the family, the little records that they had. I couldn't tell you anything about that side of the family.
And was your family all from New Orleans? Oh my daddy was from Macomb, Mississippi.

Oh, from Macomb. Okay. And my mother was from across the river. And they all moved here. Many, I mean to New Orleans many years ago. And I was born on 2909 LaSalle Street. That's right at 6 and LaSalle and Cross That was way before the projects was there. Then we moved to St. Andrew, 2620 St. Andrew Street. That's between Magnolia and Robinson, right across from the 12th Precent. That's where I had to be around nine months old. I stayed there all of my life. So you were right, yeah, at St. Andrew. Yeah, and I came in that neighborhood, yeah. St. Andrew, between Magnolia and Robinson.
Were some of your friends that you went to school with, were all of them from in that

area? Yeah, most of them. Some of them played music, some of them were just friends. And today a lot of them are professional people. We all went in different directions. But it was a close-knit neighborhood. We didn't have that much, but we were all welcome to each other's homes. And if you did something wrong, your mother didn't have to take care of somebody in the block, which was good, because it learned your discipline and respect. You know what you had to do, what you could do. So I'm thankful for that. And a lot of my partners are thankful, because we all came up during that time. Right. There wasn't much offered for opportunities during that time. But everybody went to school, and I'd say we were some professional in there all right, other than music. But it was an wholesome neighborhood with a lot of good friends, and thank God we're still friends today.
Did you feel that you had any other options as far as work besides music? Well I did some other things.
I was a rabbit on the river for a lot of times, a long time. I worked on the river. What specific?
What did you do?

Hauling them, stuff up in the holes, sacks, oyster shells. I did this with my father-in-law, this was in between jobs, music when I was married. So it's been quite a few other jobs that I've had other than music, but music has been my lifelong work. But it was a thing called survival. Like I said, you're a man first, you're a musician second.
Well Tex, I'm going to talk to your cousin Tex. Yeah, Tex Stevens, yeah. He gave me a litany of jobs. I didn't. Tex gave me a litany of jobs he had.
He cuts an album.
Yeah, exactly.

Yeah, but he was all part of it, you know. So he would be the emcee around the different clubs, and he was on the radio at the time, and he would help, especially if a guy had a record out. At that time he was going to be able to go to the record, disc jacket with your record. Right. And he'd play it right there. But now you have to get permission from the White House to get a record played, you know, music, other than a very few stations. But music, you know, like I tried to tell the students that I've had, at one time I had a little drum studio that I was teaching. And I was trying to tell them, you know, be dedicated whatever you're going to do, you know, because music is like anything else. It has its ups and downs, you know. And with a family, you need a family that can understand this particular life. Right. It's a good life, you know, but you know, like, you need somebody in your corner who can understand it because it's bad enough dealing with all the other things. And then you have to come home and somebody wants to read the Ride Act about the money,
you know.

But you have to take care of business. And I'm thankful that the Lord gave me a little strength. Like I said, I did many things besides playing drums, you know, because I knew what I had to do, be done, because I had a family.
So what did, was your family religious? Yeah, well I'm Baptist.

Oh, you're Baptist. Yeah, everybody came up in the Baptist church. Right now I don't belong to any church per se, but I carry the Lord in my chest 24 hours a day, you know. And I don't argue about religion and I don't discuss it. Everybody has their own way, you know, of believing in what they do. I respect their thoughts and I hope they respect mine, you know.
But when you were a kid, did the family march you off on Sunday to church?

Oh, we all had to go to church. And I was like, you know, this evangelist Baptist church, as Reverend Spears, that's the corner of Felicity and Willow. As a child, every Sunday we went to Bible class and to 11 o'clock service. But it wasn't something where you had to do. It wasn't admitted, you know, like if you don't go, this is going to happen. Mom, it was all in a little space, you know. But you couldn't do nothing wrong. I'm honored for that. She was on top of the case, you know. But it wasn't a thing where you can just run, even with my older brothers. Yeah. And I respect her for that and still miss her. But that was part of like childhood. You went to church, you had to go to church. I can remember if you start lighting and thunder and return off the radio, put covers over the mirror and everybody just sit down, you know. That was their way. It wasn't even thunder and lightning, you know, like the Lord speaking or whatever. But as a youngster this was part of it, so hey, you go along with it.
No regrets. So was your mother an influence on your life? Very much so, yeah. It seems that.

My father too, but my mother, she was always there for me, you know. It was always up front, you know, like don't lie to me. Tell me what it was. As a matter of fact, she died. I was always with Sam Cooke. I was home. And I had the doctor for her, because I was in and out of town. And I left and I went to Philadelphia. And we went to Uptown Theater. And I got a call that she had passed in 61. I stayed about four or five days. And I went back. I had to get back on the road. And I was in and out of town. And I was in and out of town. And I left and I went to Philadelphia. And we went to Uptown Theater. And I got a call that she had passed in 61. And I came home for the funeral.
I stayed about four or five days.

And I had to get back on the road. My father died in 1950. As a matter of fact, I was playing music then. I was playing at the old place called the Pentagon. And I was playing at the old place called the Pentagon. And I was playing at the old place called the Pentagon. It's called the Pentagon right there at Galvis, right off of St. Bernard. We were playing, the guy came in and said, your father had passed. It looks like every time I'm playing music that's what happened. My brother. But that's life. Life is on a visit so you have to enjoy yourself. That's the way I look at it. I'm at peace with myself so that helps.
That's good. You were an only child, but did you have, how big was the house you grew up in?
Three rooms in the kitchen. Three rooms in the kitchen?
Yeah. So was it like a lot of people in one room?

Well I was on the couch. Well like I said my brothers were older so they lived, my brother had his wife and my other brother had his wife. And one of my sisters Thelma, she lived in California. So it was like my older sister and my younger sister who I was next to Cleo and my mom. And my sister wasn't really overcrowded all the time. Like I said I had the couch, I had the bed. You know it was like the living room, two bedrooms, kitchen. And at first we didn't have the indoor bath. The toilet was outside. Oh even when you were going out?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Was that a privy? Was that a privy?
Was that a privy?

I mean what was it? Oh yeah, yeah. It was connected to the house. You'd go out to the house and make a ride. Make a ride. If it rain, it was cold, you'd bring a little paper in there and warm it up. Put the fire in there. Finally built an indoor bathroom. I can remember when we first had electricity. I was very small and I thought it was a miracle because I had the lamps when I was a child. You had oil?
Yeah, and kerosene.

We had the grate, they called it the fireplace, the grate. And that was it. There was no fire, nothing wasn't popping out. There was one we put potatoes under the ashes and baked the potatoes. But then we, somebody got lucky, my daddy got a raise or something. It was electricity, it turned on about a 25 watt bulb. And that's when it was a miracle. I'm so used to the lamps.
The lamps, yeah.

But a number three tub. Back to the dew drop thing. I'd come home and take a bath and go to school. My mother had the tub. Sit in the front of the grate, not the fireplace, in the front of the grate. And I'd sit there in the number three tub and take a bath. And lay down and fix me some breakfast and I'd get up and I'd go to school.
You'd be out that late with the dude at the dew drop?

Yeah, yeah. I was waiting six nights a week. That's why I left. I didn't graduate from Booker T. I left school. Because I was making a little money at the time and it helped the family. My mother, she said I had a long talk with me and she didn't want to force me. You know, I had to play hockey and run in the streets. You know, I was working that night when I was a youngster. I was playing shows six nights a week. And what made it funny, I would see some of my teachers. You beat the roster. You beat the roster playing. Yeah, like you partied. Yeah, yeah, yeah. They all called me Albert. And the next day I'm sitting up in the class. And I'm looking at him. Falling asleep probably. Well I'm nodding. He was out cabarending the night before, you know. But that was all fun. They put him in respect to him so that was their thing. I didn't interfere. Because I was a youngster. They were grown. These were adults, you know. When I was a kid. But I was around at that particular time. And it was a good experience for me. Because I learned a lot. They set a silly young man down and said, shut up and listen. You know, like anybody else, blah, blah, blah, blah. They said, oh man, shut up. Sit down. Let me tell you. And it helped me. And I appreciate it. My dear
Did you go second lining, you follow, run after the first? I did the first line and the second line.

I don't know what the first line was, but we did it all. I used to tell my mother, because at that time we used to have the windows open. There wasn't no heck of it. We had the big fans. And I could, this is even before I started playing drums, I could feel to me, I could hear Paul Barber and Freddie Coleman, I don't know who they were, I used to see them as a kid, we all became good friends. I could hear boom, boom, boom. And I used to tell my mother, I said, my mother's a parade coming, she said, ain't no parade coming, the windows open, it would be maybe blocks away. And then boom, boom, boom, boom. And I could say at that time, they had the second line, but everybody would sit on the sidewalk and let the parade pass so you could see everybody who was playing. And then you're talking about the drumming, Freddie Coleman, Paul Barber and Happy, all these guys, all the guys at the time, it was parade masters. These guys would make a roll and it would be like you're tearing paper. And I'd be following and listening as I got to know them. I'd be with my little drummer, I'd hear something, and I'd come home and I'd try to play that. As a matter of fact, not to jump back into the early things we were talking about, like I'd say with my brother, Richard, bless him, he brought me my first set of drums. And I set the drums up, I had the snare drum and the flow tum tum, and the little tum tum on the front. But I could only play on the snare drum, I couldn't get over to the tum tum. And then everybody would come and say, why this drum is so dirty? Not dirty, I'm just from playing on the stuff. And these other two, and I said, well I wiped them off. And I started taking the pencil and marking on them like I had been playing on them. Because I couldn't, it's a million miles if you play a drum. From the snare drum to the low tum tum to the flow tum. Coordinated all that. Yeah. And I mean so you're hitting up there and hitting over there. So I eventually learned to get over there, but that was one of the things. There was drums we'd sitting up. But I used to go every night also, my mother and them, thank you, used to let me go to the movies, or to the show, we would call it, to the rich in the palace. And they would have the bands playing, they would have the vaudeville. Sure. And I would sit and listen to Pickle, who was the drummer. Andrew Jackson. Yeah, Andrew Jackson. Andrew Jackson, yeah.
All these guys. He was a drummer at the palace? He was a drummer at the palace.

He was a drummer at the palace. He was a drummer at the palace and at the rich. He said right in the front seat, as close as you and I, you know, he'd be playing. Then he used to tell me, he said, you can't do this, you know. But he was a man and I was a child. I said, I'm going to practice that, you know, not go home. We didn't have a practice pad. We made our own little practice pads. And all of this, you know, learning and being around these fellas. And then later on, through the years, he'd meet guys like Earl Palmer, Weedy Morris, and that's Edris Muhammad's brother. Yeah. Are you aware of Weedy? Yeah, I know. Yeah, I know. Okay, he died in St. Louis. You know, Chenu, Cornise, Coleman, Ed Blackwell. And one gentleman I hope somebody says something about is Wilbert Hogan. You know, nobody says anything about Wilbert Hogan. He was the first brother that I know from here to graduate from Juilliard School of Music. He went to Book of Washington. But he was a hell of a drummer. He died a few years ago. He played with everybody with different shows. As a matter of fact, when I came back from Lionel Hampton, we were in New York, 50, late, 56, 57. He'd take my place with Hampton.
Did he go with Hampton? Yeah.

Because I said, man, you want to die? No, I don't want to deal with Hampton. We were in New York. And I came home. And the next thing I knew I got a word that Wilbert was playing with him. But he played with everybody. And he was a very dear friend. But nobody mentions his name, I hope. Remember that name, New Orleans.

You know what, a lot of guys who went on the road, and Earl King would do this to me, I'll be with him and he'll say, see that guy, he's a great saxophone player. Nobody knows what, because he was always, they left. They were always gone. Yeah. So we don't, for the cats who stayed, like Red Tyler, Red didn't go on the road a lot. He was on sessions, but we know him from his records he was on.

Well that's why one of the things I used to say, if we would all leave, we wouldn't have anybody say hello to when we come back. You know what I'm saying? Everybody was leaving in the 50s and early 60s, according to California and other places. And there's a lot of people that, somebody would be talking about musicians, they'd say, well I've never heard of him. They'd say, well he's been here all his life. He played. There's quite a few guys. Harry Nance, the drummer. Been everywhere twice, played with a lot of people. New Orleans we take it for granted. We respect the musicians, but we just take it for granted. Oh I saw him yesterday on the Do Man's trailer. Yeah, I was in the wash of Red with him. And to get the support that the guys need for local talent, and to get the support that the guys need for local talent. It's very hard, you know. Everybody loves a winner after something happened or a guy died. Everybody know him, you know. But I try to get out and support the local talent.
How important was the radio? Did you listen to radio a lot as a kid?

Yeah, well, I came up with this, you know, like Jack the Cat. These guys used to play, this was before W-Y-L, D-W-M-R-Y, all the so-called black stations came on there. You had, it was limited, and it was rhythm and blues. Yeah. It wasn't rock and roll, you know, so it was limited. But you would catch some of the music that would play the rhythm and blues. But then I lived across the street from some juke joints, and all night long they played the blues. I could hear T-Bone Walker, Lil Green, Blue Lou Barker from around the different ballrooms, you know. I mean I could be in bed at night and either a guy be coming down the street with the banjo, I mean the guitar, over his shoulder, and he'd just stop and sing the blues. I know about lived the blues, had the blues, had the blues, and played the blues. Yeah, so I mean, but like I said, it was just, then people started putting towels on music, you know. But basically it was all rhythm and blues.
What about phonograph records? Did you have a, was there a phonograph in your house?
Yeah, yeah. Graphenola. Graphenola.
One of those ones that you brought up in your hand?

Yeah, yeah. We had a lot of 78 Dr. Clayton records. Oh Dr. Clayton. Yeah. So all of the early big bands, I don't know what happened. Like I said, because we always had a piano at my house. It was always champion Jack Dupree used to stop by and play. Dupree? Oh yeah, he was good friends of my family. And he'd come in town, and when he lived here he would stay at my house. Really? Yeah, it was all like part of the family. I ran into him in Montrose, Switzerland a few years ago. He just died. Yeah, I know. But it was all part of the family.
Were you related to Dupree too?
Well, not blood, just at my house so much he'd always say we were family. You know, like I said you're my cousin, you know, because he'd come visit you so much.
Well how did he know your family?

Well he knew my mother and them before he knew me. He knew my sisters, he knew my brothers. They knew him so long ago. I don't remember when they met. Like I said, it's like I know people in New Orleans. We've just been friends. So long I can't just say, okay one day I was on the corner and he came up. He was always there. And he would play the piano and all the neighbors would come. Miss Gordon always had something going on musically at the house. Nobody played music. But the piano was there.
Well I must have been experienced to listen to Champion Jack.

I sit right there and listen to all of it. Not only him, Toots Washington used to stop by. Toots? Yeah, Papa Yellow. Yeah, he touched. Yeah, that was my man, God bless him. And all of these guys, like I said, they had a smile and lures. I was very young and these guys would come and get me and it was an experience. And they all tell my mother, they'd take care of me. We used to go like the slide out, we'd make three dollars, five dollars for that night. Not be a child, you know, with these men. But they would all bring me home. They'd pay me just like they paid the other guys.
You would go with Champion Jack? Yeah, I would go with Jack.
It was really like the slide out of the home within the neighboring town. So yeah. Like I said, they would all look out for June and I appreciate it. But it was.
Did you hear anything in Jack's music that would influence drumming? Because he seemed to be a very rhythmic player.
Yeah, just, not necessarily drumming. I just, whatever you would play, I knew a back beat would fit into it, you know. I can't recall all of the tunes I have, some of the tapes that he even sent me.
You know. But I didn't recall it.

When we went and when I ran across him in Montrose, Switzerland, he didn't know I was there with Wallace Dembo, as a matter of fact. Oh, okay. With Wallace. And when he tamed me, he started crying because he wanted to hire me to play with him. But, you know, Pirelli, what's his name, Pirelli? What? The drummer, I can't call his name, Pirelli Pirelli. Bernard Pirelli. Bernard Pirelli. Bernard Pirelli. Was playing with him. Oh, Bernard, okay. Yeah. You know, but he wanted me, he didn't know I was going to be over there, you know. And that was like, when I treated him, that was the first time I treated him, it had been about ten years. But he communicated with my family. Sure. You know. So I'm about to show you some of the pictures, you know. I'm going to come back up, you know, one day.
You're going to do that, yeah. Someday tell me and we'll do a look at photographs or something.
Yeah, and recall some things. That would be great. Yeah, but he, like I said, that was a great music experience in my life, just to have him around playing the piano.

Oh, man, that's unbelievable. I mean, I know with Toots, because I used to hang out with Toots a lot and listen to Toots a lot. Play the Jungle Blues. Play the Jungle Blues. Yeah, but I can imagine what Dan Dupree was like. Yeah. That would be like, you know, Professor Longhair.

I think with his voice, big record he had, he came back here to the house. Uh-huh. Not Honey Horse. He had a record out, it made a little noise. I mean, when I say noise, it sold a few records. Mr. Bear?
I mean, that song?

No. I mean, I'm getting a little bit of a record. See, and the police stopped him, but he didn't have a break tag or something. And he was saying, I'm champion Jack Dupree. Oh, man, I can't think of that number. I'm going to have to call you and tell you about it.
I'm trying to look it up.

But it was one of his big records. He was even kind of big in New Orleans. And that Honey Horse, Shake Baby. Shake Baby? Shake Baby. Okay. Yeah. That was it. That was it. See, I got that record out Shake Baby. That was a big record for him. He got a little recognition. That's before he moved to Germany. And I can say that was another experience that I'm grateful for.
How much, what, I'm looking at, was Mardi Gras Day a big day for you? Yeah. For your family when you were growing up or for you?

Yeah, well for me as a kid it was a great day because we used to go to, my daddy used to bring me to the old bayou just before you get to the train station that used to be. I forgot what it was, I was a child. That's where the floats used to come out on Galleup Street and they used to come through that little bayou there. I can remember that. And where I lived at all, well the wrecks would always come up Felicity Street, just come up, Claybone, Felicity to St. Charles. And all the Indians would pass and the Zulus with their time were in a limited area but they would pass right up at Great Trugate, Jackson Street and everything passed on St. Andrea and Magnolia. Right. So I mean it was a big day and everybody had a big pot of food and it was just big fun. Even as a kid I masked a few times. Where'd your mask at? Just as a clown, not as an Indian or anything but it was just fun.
Did you know the Indians? Oh yeah.

And all in the neighborhood. Different guys. Remember when you were? And they were Chilch and Wow Magnolia. Wow Magnolia. Yeah. Chief Fletcher, Bozo, Clarence Davis, all these, Big Bob. This was a big thing. I'm sorry I'm stuck for names. I know. All I'm like the guys would be making the uniforms and come by my mom and she would help. It was like everything happened. In the neighborhood. On Magnolia. Everything passed at one time. That was just another part of the city. But all you'd do was stand right there. Like I said you'd see Rex passed, you'd see Zulu passed, you'd see the Indians. And a lot of people were masked and they'd see the baby dolls and the chicks used to, it's a lot of funny things. You would fall out laughing just seeing the people don't mask as much as they used to. But I mean in the neighborhoods people would mask. And it was big fun. And it was pretty safe. I guess it was wild then but it was safe. You know you leave your door unlocked and come back. Nobody mess with your stuff, that type of thing. But I enjoyed it. Some people say, Geraldine, you were never a child. I say, yeah, because I've been playing music most of my life. I say, yeah, but I enjoyed it all. I had a chance to play with a lot of friends. We were still around. And we can reminisce about a lot of things. And we still do.
I saw something where it said you were referred to as the Amazing June Gardner.

segments.title: Opening of reel one and start of reel two

segments.chapter: Reels 1-2: Roy Brown, clubs and Sam Cooke
segments.title: Back with Roy Brown after the service, 1953-55
segments.summary: Gardner returns to Roy Brown's band after the service; changing players, jazz versus blues, and a tight band playing before Brown sang.

segments.chapter: Reels 1-2: Roy Brown, clubs and Sam Cooke
segments.title: New Orleans club work, then joining Sam Cooke in 1960
segments.summary: Mid-1950s clubs and balls in New Orleans, nine jobs a week, then the call to join Sam Cooke in 1960 and staying until Cooke's death.

segments.chapter: Reels 1-2: Roy Brown, clubs and Sam Cooke
segments.title: Turning down a move to Los Angeles after Cooke's death
segments.summary: He knew studio musicians in LA, including Earl Palmer, but chose to return home to his family in New Orleans.

segments.title: Parents and siblings
segments.summary: Reel three opens; his parents' names and his brothers and sisters, he being the youngest and the only survivor.

segments.title: Grandfather, birthplace and the St. Andrew Street neighborhood
segments.summary: Little known about grandparents; family origins, where he was born and raised, and the close-knit neighborhood.

segments.title: Day jobs on the river and advice on a musician's life
segments.summary: He worked on the river between music jobs, mentions Tex Stevens and radio, and advises students about dedication and family support.

segments.title: Baptist upbringing and church
segments.summary: Family religion, going to Bible class and service as a child, and his present faith.

segments.title: His mother and father and their deaths
segments.summary: His mother's influence; she died in 1961 while he was on tour with Sam Cooke, his father died in 1950 while he played the Pentagon.

segments.title: The family house: no indoor bath, first electricity
segments.summary: Crowded three-room house, outside toilet, kerosene lamps, the grate and the first electric bulb.

segments.title: Playing shows six nights a week and leaving school
segments.summary: He left Booker T. Washington before graduating to earn money playing shows, sometimes seeing his teachers at the cabarets.

segments.title: Second lines, parade drummers and his first drum set
segments.summary: He followed the first and second lines, listened to Freddie Coleman and Paul Barber, got a first set from his brother Richard, and watched Pickle at the theatres.

segments.title: Palace theatre drummers and Wilbert Hogan
segments.summary: Andrew Jackson at the Palace, drummers Earl Palmer, Weedy Morris and Ed Blackwell, and praise for Wilbert Hogan who took his place with Hampton.

segments.title: Musicians who left New Orleans and local support
segments.summary: Many players left for the road or California in the 50s and early 60s; New Orleans takes its musicians for granted and local talent needs support.

segments.title: Radio and the blues heard in the neighborhood
segments.summary: Early radio was limited to rhythm and blues; juke joints across the street played T-Bone Walker and others.

segments.title: Phonograph, piano and Champion Jack Dupree at the house
segments.summary: A Graphenola with 78s, a family piano, and Champion Jack Dupree staying at the house when in town.

segments.title: Dupree as family friend and early gigs together
segments.summary: How Dupree knew the family, other pianists like Toots Washington, and going out as a youngster to play for pay.

segments.title: Dupree's rhythm and meeting him again at Montreux
segments.summary: Whether Dupree influenced his drumming, and meeting him by surprise in Switzerland years later.

segments.title: Dupree's records, including Shake Baby
segments.summary: Gardner tries to recall Dupree's hit record, settling on Shake Baby, before Dupree moved to Germany.

segments.title: Mardi Gras as a child and the Indians
segments.summary: Watching Rex, Zulu and the Mardi Gras Indians pass in his neighborhood and masking as a clown.

segments.title: Nicknames: the Amazing June Gardner and Gentleman June Gardner
segments.summary: How he got the title the Amazing and why his album was named Gentleman June Gardner.

segments.title: End of reel three
segments.summary: The interviewer notes the tape is nearly out and plans to move on to drumming; garbled tape run-out.

segments.title: Studio sessions at Cosimo's in the 1950s
segments.summary: Reel four; recording many sessions at Cosimo's studio for $32 a day, replacing Earl Palmer, and being on records he cannot name.

segments.title: Recording groups and New Orleans drummers practicing together
segments.summary: Many groups recorded; drummers like Weedy, Smokey, Blackwell practiced together, learning before rudiments.

segments.title: Early recording conditions and integrated sessions
segments.summary: Sessions with few mics and tracks, stars recording in New Orleans, and black and white players always playing together despite stage segregation.

segments.title: The 99 Plus One album and Mustard Greens
segments.summary: His own album with a big band including James Booker and George Davis, recorded at Cosimo's.

segments.title: Sessions with Allen Toussaint, including Working in the Coal Mine
segments.summary: He drummed on the original Working in the Coal Mine, and the interviewer asks about overdubs and a Coca-Cola commercial.

segments.title: Later recordings with Albert King and staying out of the business
segments.summary: His last session was with Albert King, then he works occasionally and avoids the politics.

segments.title: Whether he is a show drummer
segments.summary: The interviewer calls him a showy drummer; he says it is natural feeling, and describes playing head jobs with qualified players.

segments.title: The New Orleans drummer feel and passing it on
segments.summary: The shared New Orleans feel is hard to describe; advice to young drummers to avoid attitude and help others.

segments.title: How to start learning drums: the bass drum and coordination
segments.summary: He tells a beginner to start with the bass drum foot, then hi-hat and hands, stressing time and coordination.

segments.title: Drummers as bandleaders
segments.summary: Drummers make good leaders, but leadership depends on personality and taking criticism.

segments.title: Practicing as a kid and now
segments.summary: He practiced a lot as a child while playing ball, and still keeps a pad.

segments.title: How he tunes his drums
segments.summary: He tunes each drum to the sound he wants, and drums become seasoned over time.

segments.title: Cowhide heads soaked overnight
segments.summary: They bought raw skins from Old Man Hall's store, soaked them overnight and mounted them.

segments.title: Tuning is individual
segments.summary: Tuning to notes is unnecessary; players differ, Idris Muhammad tunes differently, and a good drummer makes the sound.

segments.title: Snare, bass drum and keeping track of one
segments.summary: Relationship between snare and bass drum, the bass drum as heartbeat, and why New Orleans recordings emphasize snare and bass.
